title: Scope
description: Where a variable exists, how long it lives, and why that keeps big programs manageable.

items: A variable declared inside a function exists only there, from its declaration down to the closing brace.
That region is its **scope**. A variable like this is called a **local** variable.
So two functions can each have a `total`, and the two have nothing to do with each other.

steps.note: Call `show`. Inside it, `main`'s `total` cannot be seen at all.
`show` ended, so its `total` is gone. `main`'s was never touched.

content.title: Two totals, two scopes
content.outro: No function can reach into another's local variables, so a mistake in one function cannot quietly break the rest.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `change` sets its own local `x` to 2. `main`'s `x` is a different variable and stays 1.

items.title: Does not compile
items.text: `'total' was not declared in this scope`. From `show`'s point of view there is no such variable.

items.title: Pass it in
items.text: A parameter gives `show` its own copy to use.

content.title: Use a parameter, not another function's variable

content.value: Seeing `was not declared in this scope` for a variable? Ask in order: Is it declared in this function? Did I declare it inside an `if` or `for` I am now outside of? Is it another function's variable, which needs a parameter?
content.title: Three questions

content.caption: A plain parameter is local too: a local variable that arrives with a value. `countdown` counts its `n` to 0, and `main`'s `n` never moves. (A reference, `int& n`, is the exception: it names the caller's variable.)

items: Scope is about braces, not just functions. Every `{ }` makes a new scope, including an `if` or a `for` block.
Declare each variable in the **smallest** block that needs it. A variable you can see from far away can be broken from far away.

items.title: Inside: fine
items.text: `doubled` is used inside the block where it was declared.

items.title: Outside: compile error
items.text: The block ended at `}`, and `doubled` went with it.

content.title: Inside vs outside the block
content.caption: Outside the braces, `doubled` simply does not exist.
Both loops use `i` happily: the first `i` is gone before the second is born. `biggest` works because it is declared **outside** the loop, the accumulator rule from Module 5.

content.question: Where must `count` be declared to print it after the loop?
content.explain: A variable lives until the closing brace of the block it was declared in. To survive the loop, it must be declared before it.

content.value: Locals are created when a function starts and destroyed when it ends. So a local cannot remember anything between calls.

steps.note: A brand new `visits` is born at 0.
The function ended and `visits` died. Second call.

content.title: Why it never counts past 1
content.outro: Three calls, three brand new variables, three 1s. This catches everybody once.

content.caption: The fix: keep the count in `main`, where it survives. Pass it in and return the new value, or pass it by reference as here, and the `&` says openly that the function changes it. In Module 9, classes have variables that remember between calls.

content.question: What does the third call print?
content.explain: `c` is local, so every call starts it again at 0 and adds one.

items: A variable declared outside every function, at the top of the file, is a **global**. Every function below it can see it.
With `const`, nothing can change it, so sharing it is safe. SHOUTY_CASE names, as in Module 2.
A global **without** `const` can be changed by any function, so finding who broke it means reading the whole program.
The rule from now on: constants may be shared. Changing values are passed in, and handed back by `return` or a reference.

content.caption: Changing the pass mark is a one-line edit that every function picks up, and no function can change it by accident.

The Module 5 score chart, split into functions. `main` now reads like a description of the program. `average` refuses to divide by zero: the guard lives in the one function that needs it. Sample run: `2`, then `85` and `30` prints `85 | ********`, `pass`, `30 | ***`, `fail`, `Average: 57.5`. Next module: arrays and vectors, one variable holding a whole list.

quiz.question: Where does a variable declared inside a function exist?
options: Only inside that function, from its declaration to the closing brace
quiz.explain: That is its scope. Two functions can each have a `total` and they are unrelated.

quiz.question: A function tries to use a variable belonging to main. What happens?
options: A compile error, `was not declared in this scope`: pass it in as a parameter instead
It works, because main runs first
It compiles but the value is 0
quiz.explain: From inside the other function there is genuinely no such variable. A parameter is how a value crosses that boundary.

quiz.question: Why can two `for` loops in the same function both declare `int i`?
options: C++ allows duplicate names for counters
Each loop's i belongs to that loop's block and is gone before the next starts
Only if the loops count differently
quiz.explain: Every pair of braces makes a scope, so the first `i` no longer exists when the second is declared.

quiz.question: A function declares `int visits = 0;` then increments and prints it. Called three times, what does it print?
quiz.explain: Locals are created fresh on every call. To carry a value across calls, keep it in main and pass it by reference, or pass it in and return it.

quiz.question: What may reasonably be declared outside every function, at the top of the file?
options: A `const` global that every function can read but none can change
Any variable you want several functions to share
quiz.explain: Constants are safe to share because nothing can change them. Changing values should travel as parameters, return values and references.
